summary: Describes a format for LDAP Uniform Resource Locators, so a directory server, a search or an entry can be referred to by a link. It replaces RFC 1959 and was replaced by RFCs 4510 and 4516.

plainLanguage.summary: An LDAP URL is a way to write down a directory lookup as a single line of text, so it can be pasted into a message or a program. It says which server to ask, which entry to start from, how widely to search, what to look for, and what to bring back.

subtitle: A link format that names an LDAP directory entry, or a whole search, the way a web address names a page.

tldr.problem: LDAP directory entries and searches had no standard way to be written down as a link that a person or program could pass around.
tldr.mechanism: An LDAP URL starts with ldap:// and packs a server, a base distinguished name, attributes, a scope, a filter and optional extensions into one string, separated by question marks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2255 has been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4516. It updated the LDAP URL format for version 3 of LDAP and replaced RFC 1959, and it added an extension mechanism so later documents could add features.

today: RFC 2255 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4516, and it was itself updated by RFC 3377. It replaced RFC 1959.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. This document describes a format for an LDAP Uniform Resource Locator. The format describes an LDAP search operation to perform to retrieve information from an LDAP directory. It replaces RFC 1959, updates the LDAP URL format for version 3 of LDAP, and clarifies how LDAP URLs are resolved. It also defines an extension mechanism for LDAP URLs, so that future documents can extend their functionality, for example to provide access to new LDAPv3 extensions as they are defined.

The note at the top of the document warns that until mandatory authentication mechanisms are standardized, clients and servers written to this specification that use update functionality are unlikely to interoperate, or may interoperate only if authentication is reduced to an unacceptably weak level. Implementors are discouraged from deploying LDAPv3 clients or servers that implement update functionality until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication in LDAPv3 has been approved and published as an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: An LDAP URL is a way to write down a directory lookup as a single line of text, so it can be pasted into a message or a program. It says which server to ask, which entry to start from, how widely to search, what to look for, and what to bring back.

sections.title: The URL Grammar
sections.content:
An LDAP URL begins with the protocol prefix ldap and is defined by the following grammar.

ldapurl    = scheme "://" [hostport] ["/"
             [dn ["?" [attributes] ["?" [scope]
             ["?" [filter] ["?" extensions]]]]]]
scheme     = "ldap"
attributes = attrdesc *("," attrdesc)
scope      = "base" / "one" / "sub"
extensions = extension *("," extension)
extension  = ["!"] extype ["=" exvalue]

The ldap prefix indicates an entry or entries residing in the LDAP server running on the given hostname at the given port number. The default LDAP port is TCP port 389. If no host and port are given, the client must have some prior knowledge of an appropriate LDAP server to contact.

The dn is an LDAP Distinguished Name using the string format of RFC 2253. It identifies the base object of the LDAP search.

The attributes construct indicates which attributes should be returned from the entry or entries. If it is omitted, all user attributes of the entry or entries should be requested, by setting the attributes field of the search request to a null list, or in LDAPv3 by requesting the special attribute name *.

The scope construct specifies the scope of the search to perform in the given LDAP server. The allowable scopes are base for a base object search, one for a one-level search, or sub for a subtree search. If scope is omitted, a scope of base is assumed.

The filter specifies the search filter to apply to entries within the specified scope during the search, in the format of RFC 2254. If it is omitted, a filter of (objectClass=*) is assumed.

Any URL-illegal characters, such as spaces, URL special characters as defined in RFC 1738, and the reserved character ? (ASCII 63) occurring inside a dn, filter, or other element of an LDAP URL MUST be escaped using the percent method described in RFC 1738. If a comma occurs inside an extension value, the character MUST also be escaped that way.
sections.plainLanguage: The link is built like an address with optional extras: which phone book, which entry, which details you want, how widely to look, and any special conditions. Leave out the extras and the computer uses sensible defaults.

sections.title: Extensions and the Bindname Extension
sections.content:
The extensions construct provides the LDAP URL with an extensibility mechanism, allowing the capabilities of the URL to be extended in the future. Extensions are a simple comma-separated list of type=value pairs, where the value portion MAY be omitted for options that do not require it, and each pair is a separate extension. These LDAP URL extensions are not necessarily related to any of the LDAPv3 extension mechanisms. Extensions may be supported or unsupported by the client resolving the URL. An extension prefixed with a ! character, ASCII 33, is critical; one without it is non-critical.

The rules are explicit. If an extension is supported by the client, the client MUST obey the extension if it is critical, and SHOULD obey supported extensions that are non-critical. If an extension is unsupported by the client, the client MUST NOT process the URL if the extension is critical, and MUST ignore the extension if it is unsupported and non-critical. If a critical extension cannot be processed successfully by the client, the client MUST NOT process the URL; if a non-critical extension cannot be processed successfully, the client SHOULD ignore the extension.

Extension types prefixed by X- or x- are reserved for use in bilateral agreements between communicating parties. Other extension types MUST be defined in this document, or in other standards-track documents.

One extension is defined in this document. The bindname extension represents the distinguished name for a client to use when authenticating to an LDAP directory during resolution of an LDAP URL, and clients MAY implement it. Its value is the distinguished name of the directory entry to authenticate as, in the same form as the dn in the grammar above, and the dn may be the empty string to specify unauthenticated access. The extension may be either critical or non-critical.

If the bindname extension is critical, the client resolving the URL MUST authenticate to the directory using the given distinguished name and an appropriate authentication method. Note that for an empty distinguished name, no bind may be required to obtain anonymous access to the directory. If the extension is non-critical, the client MAY bind to the directory using the given distinguished name.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions are optional notes on the link. A note marked with an exclamation mark means: follow this or do not open the link at all. Unmarked notes can be skipped if you do not understand them. The one note defined here is the identity to authenticate as.

sections.title: Resolving an LDAP URL
sections.content:
First, the client obtains a connection to the LDAP server referenced in the URL, or to an LDAP server of the client's choice if no server is explicitly referenced. The connection MAY be opened specifically for the purpose of resolving the URL, or the client MAY reuse an already open connection. The connection MAY provide confidentiality, integrity or other services, for example using TLS, and the use of security services is at the client's discretion if not specified in the URL.

Next, the client authenticates itself to the LDAP server. This step is optional, unless the URL contains a critical bindname extension with a non-empty value. If a bindname extension is given, the client proceeds as described earlier. If a bindname extension is not specified, the client MAY bind to the directory using a distinguished name and authentication method of its own choosing, including no authentication at all.

Next, the client performs the LDAP search operation specified in the URL. Additional fields in the LDAP protocol search request, such as sizelimit, timelimit, deref, and anything else not specified or defaulted in the URL specification, MAY be set at the client's discretion.

Once the search has completed, the client MAY close the connection to the LDAP server, or MAY keep it open for future use.
sections.plainLanguage: To follow the link, your computer connects to the directory, maybe shows an ID, asks the question written in the link, and then either hangs up or stays on the line for next time.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The document gives several worked URLs. ldap:///o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US names an entry on a server of the client's choosing, and the same with ldap.itd.umich.edu after ldap:// names it on a particular server. Both correspond to a base object search of that entry using a filter of (objectclass=*), requesting all attributes.

The next example asks only for the postalAddress attribute of the same entry. A further example queries a server on port 6666 and does a subtree search of the University of Michigan for any entry with a common name of Babs Jensen, retrieving all attributes: ldap://host.com:6666/o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US??sub?(cn=Babs%20Jensen). Another example refers to all children of the c=GB entry: ldap://ldap.itd.umich.edu/c=GB?objectClass?one, where the objectClass attribute is requested and the default filter is used.

One example illustrates the escaping mechanism on the reserved character, retrieving the mail attribute for the entry named o=Question?,c=US as ldap://ldap.question.com/o=Question%3f,c=US?mail. Another shows the interaction between LDAP and URL quoting: ldap://ldap.netscape.com/o=Babsco,c=US??(int=%5c00%5c00%5c00%5c04). The filter uses the LDAP escaping mechanism of the backslash to encode three zero bytes in the value, which in LDAP would be written as (int=\00\00\00\04); because the backslash must be escaped in a URL, each one becomes %5c.

The final examples show the bindname extension: ldap:///??sub??bindname=cn=Manager%2co=Foo and ldap:///??sub??!bindname=cn=Manager%2co=Foo. The two are the same except that the second marks the extension as critical, and the comma in the distinguished name value is escaped as %2c.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show real-looking links, such as asking one university's directory for just its postal address, or asking a server on an unusual port for everything under one entry with a given name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general URL security considerations of RFC 1738 are relevant for LDAP URLs.

The use of security mechanisms when processing LDAP URLs requires particular care, since clients may encounter many different servers via URLs, and since URLs are likely to be processed automatically, without user intervention. A client SHOULD have a user-configurable policy about which servers to connect to using which security mechanisms, and SHOULD NOT make connections that are inconsistent with this policy.

Sending authentication information, whatever the mechanism, may violate a user's privacy requirements. In the absence of specific policy permitting authentication information to be sent to a server, a client should use an anonymous connection. Some authentication methods, in particular reusable passwords sent to the server, may reveal easily abused information to the remote server or to eavesdroppers in transit, and should not be used in URL processing unless explicitly permitted by policy. Confirmation by the human user of the use of authentication information is appropriate in many circumstances, and the use of strong authentication methods that do not reveal sensitive information is much preferred.

The LDAP URL format allows the specification of an arbitrary LDAP search operation to be performed when evaluating the URL. Following an LDAP URL may cause unexpected results, for example the retrieval of large amounts of data or the initiation of a long-lived search. The security implications of resolving an LDAP URL are the same as those of resolving an LDAP search query.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can make your computer ask a stranger's directory a big question, so your computer should follow your own rules about whom to talk to and what to reveal.

data.title: LDAP URL grammar
data.code:
ldapurl    = scheme "://" [hostport] ["/"
             [dn ["?" [attributes] ["?" [scope]
             ["?" [filter] ["?" extensions]]]]]]
scheme     = "ldap"
attributes = attrdesc *("," attrdesc)
scope      = "base" / "one" / "sub"
extensions = extension *("," extension)
extension  = ["!"] extype ["=" exvalue]

items.label: Base object
items.desc: Search only the named entry. This is the default when scope is omitted.

items.label: One level
items.desc: Search the entries one level below the named entry.

items.label: Subtree
items.desc: Search the named entry and everything beneath it.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH PART OF THE URL DOES

items.title: hostport
items.text: Which server to ask. The default is TCP port 389.

items.title: dn
items.text: The distinguished name of the entry the search starts from.

items.title: attributes
items.text: Which attributes to bring back. Omitted means all user attributes.

items.title: scope
items.text: How widely to search: base, one or sub. Omitted means base.

items.title: extensions
items.text: Extra conditions, such as the identity to authenticate as.
